sections.h2: What should you know before selling a house in Zanesville, Ohio?
sections.html:
Zanesville is the Muskingum County seat, built where the Licking River meets the Muskingum River about 52 miles east of Columbus. The Census Bureau estimates 25,138 residents as of July 1, 2025, up 1.4% from the April 2020 estimates base of 24,783 after decades of decline from a peak of 40,517 in 1950.

The city is named for Ebenezer Zane, whose pioneer trail crossed the Muskingum here, and it served as Ohio's second state capital from 1810 to 1812. The National Road, now U.S. 40, runs through town alongside Interstate 70, and U.S. 22 and state routes 60 and 93 also pass through. The three-way Y-Bridge over the river junction is on the National Register of Historic Places.

Zanesville was once known for pottery. Weller, Roseville and J. B. Owens operated here in the first half of the twentieth century, drawing on local clay deposits. The city peaked economically in the 1950s, and Wikipedia describes its present economy as having relatively high poverty and low labor force participation.

sections.h2: What do the Census figures say about the Zanesville housing market?
sections.html:
Zanesville is a renter-heavy city. Census QuickFacts for 2020 to 2024 shows only 43.8% of homes owner-occupied, the lowest of the four cities in the table, with a median owner-occupied value of $123,700 and a median gross rent of $821.

  • There are 10,601 households averaging 2.28 people.
  • Median household income is $43,280, and 24.1% of residents are in poverty.
  • 15.1% of adults 25 and older have a bachelor's degree, and 85.4% have at least a high school diploma.
  • Mean travel time to work is 22.8 minutes.
  • Health care and social assistance receipts were about $1.01 billion in 2022, and retail sales were about $907 million, or $36,876 per resident, the highest of the four cities.

With fewer than half of homes occupied by owners, tenants are part of many sales. If your house has a tenant, tell buyers whether the lease runs past closing and who holds the deposit.

sections.h2: Which schools, colleges and hospitals serve Zanesville?
sections.html:
Most students inside the city limits attend Zanesville City Schools, with Zanesville High School as the high school. Small northern portions of the city fall in the West Muskingum and Tri-Valley local school districts, so confirm the district for your parcel before you advertise it. Private options include Bishop Rosecrans High School and Zanesville Christian School.

Higher education is local. Ohio University Zanesville is a branch campus of Ohio University, and Zane State College sits next to it. Muskingum University is in nearby New Concord. In 2016 the Good Samaritan and Bethesda campuses merged to form Genesis Hospital, and Good Samaritan was closed and demolished.

sections.h2: How does Zanesville's building and code enforcement office affect a sale?
sections.html:
The city's Building and Code Enforcement office, at 401 Market Street, Room 227, enforces the International Property Maintenance Code, the city's codified ordinances and the zoning code, and it can start legal proceedings against violators. It is open Monday through Friday from 7:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and its phone number is 740-617-4890.

The office also issues and inspects the permits a buyer's inspector will ask about:

  • Residential building, electrical and mechanical permits, which do not include plumbing.
  • Residential and commercial sidewalk, curb and curb cut permits.
  • Demolition permits.
  • Permits to move a house or an accessory structure wider than 14 feet or larger than 450 square feet.
  • Certificates of occupancy.

The office keeps lists of condemned properties and posts a 2026 annual vacant property form among its code enforcement forms. If your house is vacant, ask the office whether the form applies before you list it. For zoning questions, the county auditor's page lists the city's Planning and Zoning office at 740-617-4909. South Zanesville has its own permit department at 740-454-0492, which matters if your address is just outside the city line.

sections.h2: How do Muskingum County values, appeals and homestead rules work?
sections.html:
The Muskingum County Auditor's office is at 401 Main Street in Zanesville and answers at (740) 455-7109, Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The auditor explains that the January 2026 tax bills reflect values set in January 2025, and that an addition, a demolition or newly passed levies can change a bill.

The Board of Revision, made up of the auditor, the treasurer and the president of the county commissioners or their designees, can change values but not tax dollars. Complaints are filed with the auditor between January 1 and March 31, and the filing starts a legal proceeding. Ohio generally allows one complaint per three-year period, and a withdrawn complaint still counts. Several details help a seller:

  • The owner carries the burden of proof, and the board can raise a value as well as lower it.
  • Hearing notice comes by certified mail at least ten days ahead.
  • An appraiser may inspect after filing and offer a settlement value. If you accept it in writing, the hearing is waived.
  • Corporations should have an attorney file for them.

The auditor's brochure for tax year 2025 explains the Homestead Exemption for seniors, disabled owners and surviving spouses. It prints a $29,000 reduction in taxable market value, an income limit of $41,000 that is adjusted annually for inflation, a December 31 filing deadline, and a larger reduction for disabled veterans equal to the tax on up to $58,000 of market value. A seller who receives the exemption should ask the auditor how a sale affects it on that parcel.

sections.h2: What must a Zanesville seller tell the buyer?
sections.html:
Under Ohio Revised Code 5302.30, a seller of a one to four unit home fills out the state disclosure form and delivers a signed copy to each prospective buyer as soon as practicable. The form asks about the water supply, sewer, structure, hazardous materials and known defects. A buyer who receives it after signing has a short window to rescind, and a seller is not liable for an error the seller did not actually know about.

Gather permit numbers and any notices from the code office before showings, so the buyer sees them with the form.

sections.h2: When does a cash offer make sense for a Zanesville house?
sections.html:
A cash offer makes sense for a rental with a tenant problem, an inherited house, or a property with open repairs that a lender's appraiser would flag. It can also help when a vacant house is costing you taxes and utilities each month.

Get more than one offer, ask who pays closing costs, and have the closing date in writing. Ask the title company to send the settlement statement a day or two ahead of the signing.

faqs.q: Who do I call about zoning in Zanesville?
faqs.a: Call the city's Planning and Zoning office at 740-617-4909. The Muskingum County Auditor lists that number, along with separate contacts for South Zanesville and several townships, because zoning is local and varies by address.

faqs.q: How often can I appeal my Muskingum County property value?
faqs.a: Ohio generally allows one complaint per three-year period. Complaints go to the county auditor between January 1 and March 31, and withdrawing a complaint still counts as the filing for that period.

faqs.q: Can the Board of Revision raise my value?
faqs.a: Yes. The county says the owner carries the burden of proof and the board may increase, decrease or leave the value unchanged. Bring a recent sale, an appraisal or repair estimates.

faqs.q: Does a vacant Zanesville house need to be registered?
faqs.a: The city's code enforcement page lists an annual vacant property form for 2026. Call Building and Code Enforcement at 740-617-4890 to learn whether your address must file before you sell.

faqs.q: What permits might a buyer ask me about in Zanesville?
faqs.a: A buyer's inspector may ask about residential building, electrical and mechanical permits, demolition permits and certificates of occupancy, all issued by the city's Building and Code Enforcement office. Bring permit numbers for any addition or major system replacement.
